question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in (-\pi ,\pi ].$ Given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )
$$

and ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0$ at $\theta =0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(0)=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0$

III. The curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =0$

*Hint: It is not necessary to use L'Hopital's rule to evaluate the limit in part II.*
question.worked_solution:
When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =0$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Computing the limit, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{{sin}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{2\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)(3{cos}^{2}⁡(0)-{sin}^{2}⁡(0))}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (3\cdot 1-0)}{2\cdot 1\cdot 1} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since the limit in part II equals $0,$ there curve has a horizontal tangent at $\theta =0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227801/assets/a48593a3bbcc61afaf80de619be505cb6dac58c559e03a0eab4553bd5a1e5013.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
